intro: The United Kingdom was built by joining England, Wales, Scotland and Ireland over hundreds of years. It became the first industrial nation and ruled the largest empire in history, and its ideas about parliament, law and sport spread around the world.

chapters.title: Stone circles, Celts and Romans
text: People have lived in Britain for hundreds of thousands of years, coming and going as ice ages came and went. After the last one, rising seas cut Britain off from mainland Europe around 8,000 years ago, turning it into an island.

Farmers built huge monuments. The great stones of Stonehenge in southern England were raised around 2500 BC, and nobody knows for certain what the circle was for. Later, Celtic-speaking peoples lived in tribes across Britain and Ireland.

In AD 43 the Romans invaded and made most of what is now England and Wales a province called Britannia. They founded Londinium, today's London, and around AD 122 Emperor Hadrian began a wall across the north to mark the edge of Roman rule. The Romans never conquered Scotland or Ireland, and their army left Britain around 410.

highlight.title: Why it matters
highlight.text: Many British towns still carry Roman names. Places ending in -chester or -caster, such as Manchester and Lancaster, grew from Roman forts; the word comes from the Latin castra, 'camp'.

chapters.title: Anglo-Saxons and Vikings
text: After the Romans left, Angles, Saxons and Jutes from what is now Germany and Denmark settled in eastern and southern Britain. England takes its name from the Angles, and their language, Old English, is the ancestor of modern English. Britons kept their own languages and kingdoms in the west, including Wales and Cornwall.

From 793, when raiders attacked the monastery of Lindisfarne, Vikings from Scandinavia raided and then settled much of northern and eastern England. King Alfred the Great of Wessex fought them off in the south, and his descendants united the English kingdoms into one: England, in the 900s.
In the north, the kingdom that became Scotland formed from several peoples, including the Picts and Gaels.

chapters.title: Normans, Magna Carta and Parliament
text: In 1066 William, Duke of Normandy, defeated the English king Harold at the Battle of Hastings. The Normans built castles across England, gave land to their followers and made French the language of the rulers for centuries. In 1086 William ordered the Domesday Book, a survey of who owned what across England.

In 1215 rebel barons forced King John to agree to Magna Carta, the 'Great Charter'. It said that even the king had to obey the law. Over the next century, kings began calling meetings of nobles, churchmen and representatives of towns to approve taxes: the start of Parliament.
English kings conquered Wales in the 1280s. They also tried to conquer Scotland, but the Scots under Robert the Bruce won a famous victory at Bannockburn in 1314 and stayed independent.

highlight.title: Why it matters
highlight.text: Magna Carta became a symbol of the idea that rulers are under the law. Its ideas inspired later documents such as the American Bill of Rights.

chapters.title: Tudors, Stuarts and a civil war
text: King Henry VIII broke with the Pope in the 1530s so that he could end his first marriage, and made himself head of a new Church of England. His daughter Elizabeth I ruled for 45 years; in 1588 her navy defeated the Spanish Armada, a huge invasion fleet. Her reign is also the age of William Shakespeare.
When Elizabeth died in 1603 without children, King James VI of Scotland also became King James I of England. The two countries now shared a king, though they kept separate parliaments.

Arguments between kings and Parliament over money and religion led to civil war in the 1640s. Parliament won, King Charles I was executed in 1649, and for 11 years there was no king. The monarchy returned in 1660, but after the 'Glorious Revolution' of 1688 the Bill of Rights of 1689 made sure Parliament, not the monarch, had the final say.

chapters.title: Union and empire
text: In 1707 the Acts of Union joined England (which already included Wales) and Scotland into one Kingdom of Great Britain with a single parliament in London. In 1801 Ireland was added, creating the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland.

Britain built a global empire through trade, settlement and war. It lost its American colonies, which became the United States, in 1783, but gained India, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and large parts of Africa and Asia. By the early 1900s the British Empire ruled about a quarter of the world's land and people, the largest empire in history.

British ships carried millions of enslaved Africans across the Atlantic. After long campaigns by abolitionists, including formerly enslaved people such as Olaudah Equiano, Britain banned the slave trade in 1807 and slavery in most of its empire in 1833.

highlight.title: Two sides
highlight.text: The empire spread the English language, railways and laws, but it was built and held by force, and it caused great suffering, from famines in India to the slave trade. How to remember it is still debated in Britain today.

chapters.title: The first industrial nation
text: From the late 1700s Britain was the first country to have an Industrial Revolution. Coal-powered steam engines, improved by the Scottish engineer James Watt, drove machines in cotton mills, and factories turned towns like Manchester and Glasgow into big cities in a few decades.
The world's first public railway to use steam locomotives opened between Stockton and Darlington in 1825, and railways soon criss-crossed the country. Britain became 'the workshop of the world'.

Life in the new cities was often hard, with long hours, child labour and crowded, dirty housing. Workers formed trade unions and campaigned for the vote, which was slowly given to more men through the 1800s. Queen Victoria reigned from 1837 to 1901 over this time of rapid change.

chapters.title: Two world wars and a new Ireland
text: Britain fought in the First World War from 1914 to 1918. Hundreds of thousands of soldiers from Britain and across the empire died in the trenches of France and Belgium. In 1918 women over 30 got the vote, after years of campaigning by the suffragettes; women won the vote on equal terms with men in 1928.

In Ireland, a war of independence led to most of the island leaving the UK in 1922 as the Irish Free State, today the Republic of Ireland. Six counties in the north stayed in the UK as Northern Ireland, and the country's name became the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland.

In the Second World War Britain, led by Winston Churchill from 1940, stood against Nazi Germany. In the Battle of Britain in 1940 the Royal Air Force stopped a German invasion, but bombing raids called the Blitz killed tens of thousands of people in British cities.

chapters.title: Modern Britain
text: After 1945 a new government created the welfare state, including the National Health Service in 1948, which gives healthcare free when you need it. Most of the empire became independent, starting with India and Pakistan in 1947, and many former colonies joined the Commonwealth. People from the Caribbean, South Asia and Africa came to help rebuild Britain, starting with the arrival of the ship Empire Windrush in 1948.

From the late 1960s to 1998 Northern Ireland suffered 'the Troubles', a violent conflict that killed more than 3,500 people. The Good Friday Agreement of 1998 brought a fragile peace. In 1999 Scotland and Wales got their own parliaments, and in 2014 Scotland voted to stay in the UK.

The UK joined the European Economic Community, forerunner of the EU, in 1973. In a referendum in 2016 a narrow majority voted to leave, and the UK left the EU on 31 January 2020. Queen Elizabeth II, the longest-reigning British monarch, died in 2022 after 70 years on the throne, and her son became King Charles III.

keyTerms.meaning: A charter of 1215 that limited the king's power and said he must follow the law.
A country with a king or queen whose powers are limited by law, while elected politicians govern.
The change from making things by hand to making them in factories with machines, which began in Britain in the late 1700s.
A group of lands and peoples ruled by one country.
A voluntary association of 56 countries, most of them once part of the British Empire.
Handing some powers from the UK government to parliaments in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.
